description_full: Simon Property Group, Inc. is a self-administered and self-managed real estate investment trust (REIT). Simon Property Group, L.P., or the Operating Partnership, is our majority-owned partnership subsidiary that owns all of our real estate properties and other assets. In this package, the terms Simon, we, our, or the Company refer to Simon Property Group, Inc., the Operating Partnership, and its subsidiaries. We own, develop and manage premier shopping, dining, entertainment and mixed-use destinations, which consist primarily of malls, Premium Outlets, The Mills, and International Properties. At December 31, 2024, we owned or had an interest in 229 properties comprising 183 million square feet in North America, Asia and Europe. We also owned an 88% interest in The Taubman Realty Group, or TRG, which owns 22 regional, super-regional, and outlet malls in the U.S. and Asia. Additionally, at December 31, 2024, we had a 22.4% ownership interest in Klepierre, a publicly traded, Paris-based real estate company, which owns shopping centers in 14 European countries. Simon Property Group, Inc. was incorporated in 1960 and is based in Indianapolis, Indiana.

financial_summary: Simon Property Group, Inc. is a large-cap real estate business with a $86.7B market cap on $6.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $3.2B in free cash flow — roughly 50 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.89× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 6.0× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 3.3×.

Shareholder yield of 3.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Climate and insurance cost escalation — rising premiums and coverage withdrawals in flood/fire zones are repricing assets that the market once treated as perpetuities.

sect: Its 50% operating margin runs 27pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.50x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 1.8% of sector revenue and 4.4% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-2.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 17% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 4% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 19% and a beta of 0.92, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.09 vs 5y 0.91), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $238.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 70% in the 2020 crash, 44% in the 2022 bear market and 74% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $106 (margin of safety -115%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 53%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $69.57 to $160 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Real Estate peers: cheaper on P/E 16.5 vs 23.6, richer on EV/EBITDA 20.6 vs 16.3 and P/FCF 27.1 vs 17.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 83% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 19 covering analysts target $229 on average, in line with the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.94).
It converts 50% of revenue into free cash flow.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 50%.
ROE of 89% is amplified by 7.8x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 6.0x net debt to EBITDA ($823.1M of cash against $28.4B of debt), with interest covered 3.3x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.79 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.3% over 3 years, 6.7% over 5 years and 1.9% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 11.7% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 12.2% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (14.7% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
It has missed earnings estimates by 8.9% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.8%, and institutions hold 96%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (11 purchases, net $312K bought).
It returns 3.6% a year to shareholders (0.3% in buybacks and 3.9% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 32 consecutive years.
people: With about 3,100 employees, each generates about $2.1M of revenue, in line with the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 3.3% a year.
That works out to $1.0M of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.1M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
